title: The deceptive Dream sent by Zeus
greek: οὖλον ὄνειρον (oulon oneiron)
short: To begin honouring Achilles, Zeus sends Agamemnon a lying dream in the shape of Nestor, promising that Troy will fall that very day.
body: Oulos means 'baneful, destructive' (Leaf connects it with ollumi, 'destroy'); Leaf also notes that only this particular dream is personified, for Homer has no separate Dream-god. The Dream stands 'above his head', the usual position of dream figures in Homer (compare Patroclus' ghost, 23.68), and takes the form of the person Agamemnon most trusts, Nestor. E. R. Dodds used this scene to describe the Homeric 'objective' dream, an outside visitor rather than an inner experience. The episode troubled ancient moralists: Plato's Socrates rejects the lying dream sent to Agamemnon as unworthy of a god who cannot deceive (Republic 2.383a). Narratively it is also a fine piece of repetition: Zeus's message is repeated by the Dream and again by Agamemnon to the council (2.23-34, 56-70), so the audience hears the lie three times while knowing it is false.

title: 'Long-haired Achaeans' (karē komoōntes)
greek: κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς (karē komoōntas Akhaious)
short: A stock epithet: Greek warriors let their hair grow long all over the head, unlike some neighbours who shaved part of it.
body: Literally 'growing hair on the head'. Long hair was a mark of the free warrior; Herodotus reports that the Spartans combed their long hair before battle at Thermopylae (7.208-9). Leaf compares the Abantes of Euboea, who wore their hair 'long at the back' only (2.542), and Thracians 'with top-knots' (4.533), and suggests that the Homeric formula distinguished Achaeans, who let the hair grow everywhere, from barbarian neighbours who shaved part of the head according to tribal fashion. Like 'well-greaved', the epithet is chiefly metrical and recurs constantly (seven times in this book alone in Murray's text), but its frequency in the mouths of the Dream and of Agamemnon gives the deceptive order a heroic ring: 'arm the long-haired Achaeans'.

title: 'Fool that he was!' (nēpios): the narrator's comment
greek: νήπιος, οὐδὲ τὰ ᾔδη ἅ ῥα Ζεὺς μήδετο ἔργα (nēpios, oude ta ēidē ha rha Zeus mēdeto erga)
short: One of the rare moments when Homer's narrator judges a character: Agamemnon is a 'fool' (literally 'child'), ignorant of what Zeus intends.
body: Nēpios literally means 'infant, not yet able to speak', and so 'thoughtless, blind to what is coming'. The Homeric narrator seldom comments, so these interventions stand out; they usually come just before a character's ruin and mark the gap between what he knows and what the audience knows. Agamemnon thinks he will take Troy 'that very day'; the narrator adds that Zeus meant 'woes and groanings' for both sides. The same word judges Nastes at the end of the book, who went to war 'all decked with gold, like a girl, fool that he was' (2.872-3), and later Patroclus, who begs to fight 'great fool' (16.46). Irene de Jong's narratological study treats such comments as a key to the narrator's perspective.

title: Agamemnon's test of the army (the Diapeira)
greek: πρῶτα δ᾽ ἐγὼν ἔπεσιν πειρήσομαι, ἣ θέμις ἐστί (prōta d' egōn epesin peirēsomai, hē themis esti)
short: Agamemnon decides to 'test' the troops by proposing flight; the plan backfires as the army rushes for the ships, a famous crux of Iliadic criticism.
body: Why would a king, just promised victory, urge his men to go home? Agamemnon says this testing is 'customary' (themis), but no such custom is known, and the troops take him at his word. Leaf thought the poet was hurrying over an awkward transition 'whose exact bearing is to be forgotten as quickly as possible', and compared a story of Cortés proposing retreat to fire his men. Analyst critics saw a join between different versions; unitarians argue that the scene characterises Agamemnon's poor judgement, shows the army's war-weariness after nine years, and prepares the reversal led by Odysseus and the new resolve before the Catalogue. Studies by J. A. Russo and R. Knox (1989) and Erwin Cook (2003) explore how the test reflects Homeric conventions of leadership and speech. His speech (2.110-41), full of truth about the futile war, is itself a masterpiece of irony.

title: The bee simile
greek: ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἁδινάων (ēüte ethnea eisi melissaōn hadinaōn)
short: The army pouring to the assembly is compared to swarms of bees issuing from a hollow rock: the first of the great crowd similes.
body: The simile catches number, constant renewal ('ever coming on afresh') and clustering motion; the comparison is visual and kinetic, not moral. The epithet adinos, 'thronging', means, Leaf argues, quick and restless motion: it is used of a beating heart, of sheep, of flies, and of passionate lament. The image had a long afterlife. Virgil compares the Carthaginians building their city to bees (Aeneid 1.430-6) and the souls by Lethe to bees in a meadow (6.707-9); Milton turns it to satire when the fallen angels crowd into Pandaemonium 'as bees / In spring time' (Paradise Lost 1.768-75). In Homer the swarm is followed at once by Rumour (Ossa), 'messenger of Zeus', blazing among them (2.93-4), so the crowd is both natural and god-driven.

title: Agamemnon's sceptre and its pedigree
greek: σκῆπτρον … τὸ μὲν Ἥφαιστος κάμε τεύχων (skēptron … to men Hēphaistos kame teukhōn)
short: Instead of describing the sceptre, Homer tells its history: made by Hephaestus, passed from Zeus through Hermes to Pelops, Atreus, Thyestes and Agamemnon.
body: The sceptre is 'imperishable ever' (aphthiton, 2.46), being the work of a god, and its genealogy turns Agamemnon's authority into a gift of Zeus. Lessing, in Laocoon (ch. 16), made this the model of poetic description: Homer gives 'the history of the sceptre' rather than a picture, and he contrasts it with the dead staff by which Achilles swore in Book 1, one inherited by a king, the other carried by any judge. The list passes smoothly from Atreus to his brother Thyestes and then to Agamemnon, with no hint of the famous feud between the brothers and Thyestes' cannibal feast (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1583-1611). Thucydides used line 108, 'lord of many isles and of all Argos', as evidence for Agamemnon's naval power (1.9.4). Pausanias saw a sceptre worshipped at Chaeronea as this very object, called 'the Spear' (9.40.11-12).

title: Argeïphontes, title of Hermes
greek: διακτόρῳ ἀργεϊφόντῃ (diaktorōi argeïphontēi)
short: An ancient title of Hermes, traditionally 'slayer of Argus', the hundred-eyed guardian of Io; its real meaning was already uncertain in antiquity.
body: The traditional explanation is 'Argus-slayer', from the myth in which Hermes killed the many-eyed herdsman Argus whom Hera had set to guard Io (told, for example, in the Hesiodic Aegimius and in Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.668-721). Leaf thought the legend was later than Homer and may even have been invented to explain the name. An ancient alternative, accepted by Aristarchus, derived it from argos, 'bright, swift', and phainein, 'appear', giving 'swift-appearing' or 'bright-appearing'; Leaf found this unsatisfactory too and concluded that such names are 'inexplicable to us'. Diaktoros, Murray's 'messenger', is equally obscure (perhaps 'runner' or 'guide'). In the sceptre's genealogy Hermes stands between Zeus and the first mortal owner, Pelops, as the god who carries divine gifts to men.

title: The Icarian sea and the cornfield: similes of the rushing army
greek: κύματα μακρὰ θαλάσσης πόντου Ἰκαρίοιο (kumata makra thalassēs pontou Ikarioio)
short: Stirred by Agamemnon's test, the assembly heaves like the long waves of the Icarian Sea under East and South winds, then bends like a cornfield under the West Wind.
body: The Icarian Sea lies around the small island of Icaria near Samos in the eastern Aegean (Leaf, citing Strabo 14.1.19); later myth derived the name from Icarus, who fell there. The local precision, like the Caystrian meadow near Ephesus later in the book (2.461), is one reason scholars place the poet on or near the Ionian coast of Asia Minor. The two similes form a pair: first the crowd is a sea driven by winds 'from the clouds of father Zeus', then a field of standing grain pressed by a gust so that 'the ears bow'. Both images present a mass without will, moved by an outside force: the right tone for the panic that follows, as the men cheer, raise the dust and drag the ships toward the sea.

title: 'Beyond what was ordained' (hupermora): fate and the 'if not' moment
greek: ἔνθά κεν Ἀργείοισιν ὑπέρμορα νόστος ἐτύχθη, εἰ μὴ … (entha ken Argeioisin hupermora nostos etukhthē, ei mē …)
short: The Achaeans would have sailed home 'beyond fate' if Hera had not intervened: one of Homer's 'if not' scenes, where the story almost goes another way.
body: Hupermora means 'beyond one's portion (moira)', that is, against what destiny has fixed: the Achaeans are fated not to go home before Troy falls. Homer often uses such counterfactual 'then X would have happened, had not Y' constructions at moments of crisis (compare 3.373-5, 16.698-701, 20.30), and scholars see in them the poet showing his awareness of the tradition he must follow while making the audience feel how close events came to going differently. The relation between fate and the gods is not systematic in Homer: here the gods act to keep events on their ordained course, while elsewhere Zeus considers saving a man 'beyond fate' (16.433-43) and in the Odyssey he complains that mortals suffer 'beyond their portion' through their own folly (Od. 1.32-4). The word introduces the major theme of moira. Leaf calls hupermora 'a rhetorical expression only': nothing in Homer actually happens against fate, because a god always intervenes.

title: 'Argive Helen'
greek: Ἀργείην Ἑλένην (Argeiēn Helenēn)
short: Helen's first mention in the Iliad: 'Argive' Helen, the Greek woman whose abduction by Paris is the cause of the war and the Trojans' 'boast'.
body: 'Argive' here means Greek in the broad sense: Helen was queen of Sparta, wife of Menelaus, and Argos can stand in Homer for the Peloponnese or for Greece as a whole. Hera's words, repeated by Athena to Odysseus, make Helen the symbol of what the war is for: if the Achaeans go home they leave her to Priam as a 'boast' (eukhōlē), and the deaths of so many will have been for nothing. Nestor will likewise urge the men to stay until each has avenged 'his strivings and groanings for Helen's sake' (2.356, repeated of Menelaus at 2.590). Helen herself appears in Book 3, weaving the story of the war into a web (3.125-8) and blaming herself. Later writers questioned her guilt: Stesichorus' Palinode (cited by Plato, Phaedrus 243a-b) and Herodotus (2.112-20) claimed she never went to Troy at all, and Euripides dramatised that version in his Helen (412 BC).

anchor: the peer of Zeus in counsel
title: Odysseus, 'the peer of Zeus in counsel'
greek: Ὀδυσῆα Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον (Odusēa Dii mētin atalanton)
short: Odysseus' epithet stresses mētis, practical cunning: he is 'equal to Zeus in counsel', the man who can turn a crisis with words.
body: Mētis is the intelligence of resource and stratagem, the quality of the hero later called polumētis, 'of many wiles' (Murray's 'Odysseus of many wiles' at 1.311). Atalantos means 'of equal weight', as on a balance. In Book 2 the epithet is earned: Athena finds Odysseus grieving but motionless, sends him into action, and he takes Agamemnon's own 'staff of his fathers' to restore order, speaking gently to chiefs and roughly to commoners (2.188-206), silencing Thersites, and finally persuading the army with the memory of the portent at Aulis (2.284-332). Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant made mētis the subject of a classic study, showing its links with the goddess Metis, swallowed by Zeus, and with Athena, born of that union, which makes Odysseus' closeness to Athena natural.

title: 'No good thing is a multitude of lords': one king
greek: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη· εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς (ouk agathon polukoiraniē; heis koiranos estō, heis basileus)
short: Odysseus' rebuke to the common soldiers became the most quoted political maxim in Homer, cited by Aristotle and many later writers in support of monarchy.
body: Odysseus treats chiefs and commoners differently: to men of rank he speaks with 'gentle words', but any man of the people he strikes with the sceptre and tells to sit down and obey his betters. The authority he invokes is the king to whom Zeus has given 'the sceptre and judgments' (2.205-6). The line had a long afterlife. Aristotle closes Metaphysics book 12 (1076a4) with it, applying it to the single first principle of the universe; in the Politics (4.4, 1292a13) he discusses whether Homer meant rule by many individuals or by a collective. Christian apologists used it for monotheism, and early modern defenders of monarchy quoted it often. Modern readers note the irony that the 'one king' at this moment is the man whose foolish test caused the stampede.

title: Thersites
greek: Θερσίτης … ἀμετροεπής (Thersitēs … ametroepēs); αἴσχιστος δὲ ἀνὴρ ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθε (aiskhistos de anēr hupo Ilion ēlthe)
short: The only common soldier who speaks in the Iliad: the ugliest man at Troy, who repeats Achilles' charges against Agamemnon and is beaten by Odysseus.
body: His name, as Leaf notes, comes from the Aeolic thersos, 'boldness', a name made to fit the man; 'of measureless speech' (ametroepēs) defines his fault, talk without order (kosmos). He is described in grotesque detail: bandy-legged, lame, hunch-shouldered, with a pointed head and scant hair (2.216-19), the poem's one physical caricature. Homer names neither his father nor his country, which the scholia took as a sign of low birth, and Leaf notes he is the only common soldier named in the Iliad. Yet much of what he says echoes Achilles' own words in Book 1 (compare 2.239-42 with 1.149-71). Odysseus beats him with the golden sceptre and the army, though resentful, laughs. Critics disagree about the scene: some read it as aristocratic ideology silencing a commoner; W. G. Thalmann showed how comedy and scapegoating serve to reunite the army; Gregory Nagy related Thersites to the tradition of blame poetry. In the epic cycle Achilles later kills him for mocking his grief over the Amazon Penthesileia (Aethiopis, in Proclus' summary; also Quintus of Smyrna); Sophocles (Philoctetes 442-4), Plato (Republic 10.620c) and Shakespeare (Troilus and Cressida) all remembered him.

title: The portent at Aulis: the snake and the sparrows
greek: ἔνθ᾽ ἐφάνη μέγα σῆμα· δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινός (enth' ephanē mega sēma; drakōn epi nōta daphoinos)
short: Odysseus recalls the omen at Aulis: a blood-red snake devoured eight nestlings and their mother, and Calchas read it as nine years of war, with Troy taken in the tenth.
body: Aulis in Boeotia was where the fleet gathered before sailing to Troy. The sign comes during sacrifice under a plane-tree: a snake 'blood-red on the back' (daphoinos, which Leaf explains as 'gory, blood-red') eats the eight young sparrows and their mother, then Zeus turns it to stone. Calchas reads the nine birds as nine years. Pausanias reports that the spring was still shown at Aulis and part of the plane-tree preserved in the temple of Artemis (9.19.7, cited by Leaf). Cicero translated the passage into Latin verse and then used it to mock divination: why should sparrows signify years rather than months or days? (On Divination 2.63-5). Aeschylus gives the same campaign a darker omen at Aulis, two eagles devouring a pregnant hare (Agamemnon 104-59). Leaf also notes an echo of this line in Revelation 12:3 ('a great red dragon').

title: 'Nestor of Gerenia' (Gerēnios hippota Nestōr)
greek: Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ (Gerēnios hippota Nestōr)
short: Nestor's standing title Gerēnios is of uncertain meaning: perhaps 'of Gerenia', a place where he grew up, or a form connected with gerōn, 'old man', or geras, 'honour'.
body: Leaf sets out the ancient explanations. The traditional one, attributed to Hesiod, made it a local name from a river or town in Elis where, in that story, Nestor was brought up while exiled for a time from Pylos; but Strabo knew no such place and treated the supposed sites as fictions, while Pausanias (3.26.8) identified Gerenia with the Homeric Enope. Others took it as a lengthened form of gerōn, 'old man', or connected it with geras, 'honour'. Leaf concluded that the title was so old 'that the real meaning of it had been lost in prehistoric times'. Hippota, 'horseman', recalls Nestor's youthful exploits in chariot fighting, which he narrates at length (11.670-761). Like many Homeric epithets, it survived in the formula because it fitted the verse, not because it was understood.

title: Tribes and clans (phula, phrētrai)
greek: κρῖν᾽ ἄνδρας κατὰ φῦλα κατὰ φρήτρας (krin' andras kata phula kata phrētras)
short: Nestor advises ordering the army by tribe and 'brotherhood', so that kinsmen fight beside kinsmen and courage or cowardice can be seen.
body: Phrētrē is the same word as the Attic phratria, 'brotherhood', and is related to Latin frater; Leaf calls it 'a relic of the patriarchal time when the family, not the tribe, was the unit'. In historical Athens the phratries were hereditary associations controlling citizenship. Leaf also points out that such tactical advice is strangely out of place in the tenth year of the war and is the first of several didactic speeches given to Nestor (compare the advice to build a wall, 7.327-43); it presents him as the army's chief counsellor and leads into the Catalogue, which is itself an ordering of the army by peoples. Some critics take the passage as evidence that the Catalogue tradition was once set at the beginning of the war, at Aulis.

title: Menelaus 'came unbidden'
greek: αὐτόματος δέ οἱ ἦλθε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος (automatos de hoi ēlthe boēn agathos Menelaos)
short: Agamemnon's brother, the husband of Helen, joins the feast uninvited 'for he knew in his heart' his brother's cares: a small touch that became proverbial.
body: Menelaus, king of Sparta and Helen's husband, is the injured party of the war, yet in the Iliad he is a secondary hero: 'good at the war-cry' (boēn agathos, a formula of martial prowess also used of Diomedes), loyal, sometimes gentle, and once called a 'soft spearman' by Apollo in disguise (17.587-8). The line about his coming 'of his own accord' (automatos) was famous. In Plato's Symposium (174b-c) Socrates jokes about the proverb that good men go uninvited to the feasts of good men, and says Homer spoiled it by making Menelaus, 'a soft spearman', come uninvited to the feast of the better man Agamemnon. Homer's own explanation is simply affection: he knew 'how his brother was labouring'. Menelaus' duel with Paris in Book 3 is the first major combat of the poem.

title: Athena's aegis with its hundred golden tassels
greek: αἰγίδ᾽ ἔχουσ᾽ ἐρίτιμον ἀγήρων ἀθανάτην τε (aigid' ekhous' eritimon agērōn athanatēn te)
short: Athena carries the ageless, deathless aegis, hung with a hundred golden tassels each worth a hundred oxen, as she fills the army with the will to fight.
body: This is the first description of the aegis in the poem (compare the epithet 'aegis-bearing Zeus' in Book 1). It is called 'ageless and deathless', words otherwise used of gods themselves; Leaf took it as the storm-cloud of Zeus, imagined as an old-fashioned shield of hairy hide, whose golden tassels (thusanoi) protected and adorned its edge and later developed, in classical art, into the snakes of Athena's aegis. Its value is measured in cattle, the standard unit of worth in Homer: each tassel is hekatomboios, 'worth a hundred oxen' (compare the famous exchange of gold armour worth a hundred oxen for bronze worth nine, 6.235-6). Elsewhere the aegis bears the Gorgon's head with figures of Rout (Phobos), Strife, Valour and Onset (5.738-42), and when shaken by Zeus or Apollo it brings terror (15.229-30, 15.308-22). Here its effect is the reverse of panic: 'war became sweeter than to return' (2.453-4), a line that marks the complete reversal of the army's mood since Agamemnon's test.

title: The 'Asian meadow' and the great sequence of similes
greek: Ἀσίῳ ἐν λειμῶνι Καϋστρίου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα (Asiōi en leimōni Kaüstriou amphi rheethra)
short: Before the Catalogue, five similes in succession (fire, birds, leaves, flies, goatherds and a bull) show the gleam, sound, number, eagerness and order of the army.
body: The sequence is unique in Homer: blazing forest fire (the glare of bronze), flocks of geese, cranes and swans in the meadow by the Cayster river near Ephesus (the noise), leaves and flowers in season (number), flies around milk-pails in spring (eagerness), goatherds sorting flocks (marshalling), and finally Agamemnon as a bull pre-eminent in the herd. The 'Asian meadow' is the first appearance of the name Asia in Greek literature. Aristarchus read Asiō as the genitive of a man's name, Asias, a legendary Lydian king, which Herodotus reports the Lydians claimed as the source of 'Asia' (4.45); Virgil read it as an adjective, 'Asian' (Georgics 1.383; Aeneid 7.699-702). Leaf observes that this is the only passage in the Iliad showing detailed knowledge of the coast of Asia Minor beyond the Troad, a clue to where the poet lived.

title: The invocation before the Catalogue: 'not though ten tongues were mine'
greek: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι … οὐδ᾽ εἴ μοι δέκα μὲν γλῶσσαι, δέκα δὲ στόματ᾽ εἶεν (espete nun moi Mousai … oud' ei moi deka men glōssai, deka de stomat' eien)
short: The poet asks the Muses, who know all things, for the Catalogue: mortals 'hear but a rumour', and could not name the host even with ten tongues.
body: This is the poem's fullest statement of how epic knowledge works. The Muses are goddesses who 'are at hand and know all things', whereas 'we hear but a rumour (kleos) and know nothing' (2.485-6): the singer depends on divine memory for facts no mortal witnessed. Leaf notes that the Muses are particularly suited here as goddesses of memory (their name may share a root with Greek words for mind and memory), though their descent from Mnemosyne is post-Homeric. The 'ten tongues, ten mouths, unbreakable voice and heart of bronze' became a topos of inexpressibility: Virgil multiplies it to a hundred tongues (Georgics 2.43-4; Aeneid 6.625-7), and it reappears in many later poets. The invocation marks the Catalogue as a special, solemn kind of song.

title: The Catalogue of Ships
greek: ἀρχοὺς αὖ νηῶν ἐρέω νῆάς τε προπάσας (arkhous au nēōn ereō nēas te propasas)
short: A list of 29 Achaean contingents, their leaders, towns and ships (1,186 in all), followed by a shorter Trojan Catalogue: the most debated historical document in Homer.
body: The Catalogue moves geographically around mainland Greece and the islands, beginning unexpectedly with Boeotia, which has led many to think it was composed for the muster at Aulis and adapted to its present place. Its value as history is disputed. Denys Page and R. Hope Simpson with J. F. Lazenby argued that many of its places were inhabited chiefly in the Mycenaean age, so that it preserves Bronze Age geography; others stress post-Mycenaean elements, places no one could locate even in antiquity, and inconsistencies with the rest of the poem; Kirk's commentary surveys the debate. Thucydides already used it as evidence, estimating the army's size from the 120 men in each Boeotian ship and the 50 in Philoctetes' (1.10.4-5). Inside the poem it reviews the army at the moment it goes to war, reminds us of absent leaders (Achilles, Protesilaus, Philoctetes) and introduces many minor heroes who will die later.

title: Aias the Lesser, son of Oileus
greek: Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας μείων (Oïlēos takhus Aias meiōn); λινοθώρηξ (linothōrēx); Πανέλληνας (Panhellēnas)
short: The Locrian Aias, small, swift, in a linen corslet, is carefully distinguished from the great Telamonian Aias; the passage also contains the word 'Panhellenes'.
body: Two heroes share the name Aias (Latin Ajax): the huge Telamonian Aias of Salamis, the Achaeans' bulwark, and this smaller, fast spearman from Locris. When they fight together they are called 'the two Aiantes' (2.406). The Iliad shows him boastful and quarrelsome (23.473-98, 23.773-84); in the epic cycle he dragged Cassandra from Athena's altar at the sack of Troy (Iliupersis) and was drowned on the way home after blaspheming (Od. 4.499-511). Line 530 says he excelled 'all the Hellenes and Achaeans' (Murray's version of Panhellēnas kai Akhaious); lines 528-30 were rejected by ancient critics, as Leaf reports, both for their tautology and because Panhellēnas presupposes the later extension of the Thessalian name 'Hellenes' to all Greeks. Leaf takes linothōrēx as 'wearing a linen tunic instead of a breastplate' (Pausanias saw linen corslets at Olympia, 6.19.7), and notes that Aias does nothing in battle to justify the praise.

anchor: Aias led from Salamis twelve ships
title: Aias and Salamis: the 'Athenian interpolation'
greek: Αἴας δ᾽ ἐκ Σαλαμῖνος ἄγεν δυοκαίδεκα νῆας, στῆσε δ᾽ ἄγων ἵν᾽ Ἀθηναίων ἵσταντο φάλαγγες (Aias d' ek Salaminos agen duokaideka nēas, stēse d' agōn hin' Athēnaiōn histanto phalanges)
short: Two lines placing Aias' Salaminian ships beside the Athenians were cited in antiquity as evidence that Salamis belonged to Athens, and were accused of being an Athenian forgery.
body: The entry for the great Telamonian Aias is strangely short for so important a hero. Its second line, saying he stationed his ships 'where the battalions of the Athenians stood', was used in the sixth century BC dispute between Athens and Megara over the island of Salamis. Strabo (9.1.10) reports that some said Solon (others say Peisistratus) inserted it, and that the Megarians answered with a different version of the Catalogue; Plutarch tells the same story (Solon 10), and Aristotle mentions the Athenians' use of Homer as a witness (Rhetoric 1.15, 1375b30). The episode is one of the earliest recorded arguments about the authenticity of a Homeric line. The Athenian entry just before it (2.546-56) praises Athens' earth-born king Erechtheus and its leader Menestheus; Zenodotus rejected the praise of Menestheus (553-5) and Aristarchus line 558 as well. Leaf thought the tradition of an Athenian 'interpolation' was founded on truth, noting that Herodotus (7.161) already knew the Menestheus lines and that the praise does not fit the minor role Menestheus plays in the rest of the poem.

title: Agamemnon's hundred ships from Mycenae
greek: τῶν ἑκατὸν νηῶν ἦρχε κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων (tōn hekaton nēōn ērkhe kreiōn Agamemnōn)
short: Agamemnon brings the largest contingent, a hundred ships from Mycenae and Corinth, and even lends ships to the landlocked Arcadians: the basis of his supreme command.
body: The Catalogue makes Agamemnon's leadership concrete: he commands 'most people by far and goodliest' and outshines all the warriors because he leads the most men (2.577-80). Nestor follows with ninety ships, Diomedes and Idomeneus with eighty. Agamemnon also supplies sixty ships to the Arcadians, 'for with matters of seafaring had they naught to do' (2.612-14), a detail that fits inland Arcadia; Zenodotus marked these lines as spurious, but Leaf saw them as meant to answer a natural 'historic doubt'. Thucydides took this as evidence that Agamemnon's power rested on a fleet and on 'many islands' (1.9.3-4), and that the expedition was held together more by fear than by gratitude. The kingdom described (Mycenae, Corinth, Sicyon, the northern Peloponnese) overlaps with Diomedes' Argos, a geographical oddity often discussed by scholars of the Catalogue. Archaeologically, Mycenae 'rich in gold' (7.180, 11.46) was the greatest Bronze Age citadel of mainland Greece.

title: Thamyris, the singer punished by the Muses
greek: Μοῦσαι ἀντόμεναι Θάμυριν τὸν Θρήϊκα παῦσαν ἀοιδῆς (Mousai antomenai Thamurin ton Thrēïka pausan aoidēs)
short: At Dorion the Muses met the Thracian singer Thamyris, who boasted he could beat them in song, and in anger they 'maimed' him and took away his art.
body: This brief digression in Nestor's entry is a story about poetry inside a catalogue that has just invoked the Muses. Thamyris' offence is hubris: a mortal claiming to surpass goddesses, like Marsyas against Apollo or Niobe against Leto. The Muses made him pēros, 'maimed, disabled'; later tradition took this as blindness (Pausanias 4.33.7, and his description of Polygnotus' painting at Delphi showing Thamyris blind, his broken lyre at his feet, 10.30.8), but the word may mean a wider disabling, for they also made him 'forget his minstrelsy'. Sophocles wrote a lost Thamyras, in which he is said to have played the singer himself. Readers have often set the tale beside the blind Demodocus of the Odyssey (8.62-4), whom the Muse loved and blinded but gave sweet song: the poet's art is a dangerous gift.

title: Nireus, the handsomest man after Achilles
greek: Νιρεὺς … Νιρεὺς … Νιρεύς (Nireus … Nireus … Nireus)
short: A minor hero from Syme with only three ships, made memorable by a triple repetition of his name; Aristotle cited it as a lesson in rhetoric.
body: Each of three successive lines begins with his name (anaphora): Nireus led three ships, Nireus son of Aglaia, Nireus the most beautiful man who came to Ilios after Achilles; then the deflation, 'howbeit he was a weakling, and but few people followed with him'. Aristotle (Rhetoric 3.12.4, 1414a2) observes that by this device Homer made much of Nireus, although he never mentions him again; Leaf adds that this double repetition is unique in Homer. The name of his mother Aglaia means 'splendour', fitting his beauty. Later writers used him as the type of beauty without substance; Lucian sets him beside the ugly Thersites in the underworld, where both have become indistinguishable skulls (Dialogues of the Dead). The entry shows the Catalogue's power to sketch a character in a few words.

title: Pelasgian Argos, Phthia and Hellas: Achilles' kingdom
greek: τὸ Πελασγικὸν Ἄργος (to Pelasgikon Argos); Φθίην ἠδ᾽ Ἑλλάδα (Phthiēn ēd' Hellada); Μυρμιδόνες … καὶ Ἕλληνες καὶ Ἀχαιοί (Murmidones … kai Hellēnes kai Akhaioi)
short: Achilles' fifty ships come from southern Thessaly: 'Pelasgian Argos', Phthia and Hellas, whose people were called Myrmidons, Hellenes and Achaeans.
body: 'Argos' was a common word for a plain; 'Pelasgian Argos' was properly, Leaf argues, the central Thessalian plain around Larissa, here stretched to cover Thessaly at large, while the named towns lie in the far south around the Malian Gulf. The Pelasgians were, for later Greeks, the pre-Greek inhabitants of the land. Leaf suspected that Achilles once ruled all Thessaly, and that Hellenes, Myrmidons and Achaeans were three distinct tribes under him. Hellas here is a small district near Phthia, and the Hellenes a local people; Thucydides (1.3.2-3) saw in this passage proof that the name 'Hellenes' spread from this region only later to all the Greeks, and that Homer never used it for the whole army. The Catalogue entry is also a reminder of Achilles' absence: his men 'bethought them not of war', for he lay idle in anger over Briseis, whom he had taken from Lyrnessus when he sacked it and Thebe (2.686-93). The narrator adds 'but soon was he to arise again' (2.694), a prolepsis of Book 19.

title: Protesilaus, the first to die at Troy
greek: Πρωτεσίλαος ἀρήϊος (Prōtesilaos arēïos); ἀμφιδρυφὴς ἄλοχος (amphidruphēs alokhos); δόμος ἡμιτελής (domos hēmitelēs)
short: Leader of the Thessalians of Phylace, killed by a Dardanian as he leapt ashore 'by far the first of the Achaeans', leaving a grieving wife and a 'half-finished' house.
body: His name was understood as 'first of the people' or 'first to leap', and the Iliad dramatises it: he was the first Achaean to land and the first to be killed. The Cypria named his killer as Hector. In two lines Homer sketches a whole tragedy: his wife, cheeks torn in mourning (amphidruphēs, explained by Leaf from 11.393, the torn cheeks of a widow), left at Phylace, and the house 'half-completed' (hēmitelēs), perhaps meaning unfinished, perhaps a marriage without children. Later poets gave the wife a name, Laodamia, and a story of love beyond death: Euripides' lost Protesilaus, Catullus 68.73-130 and Ovid's Heroides 13. Herodotus describes his hero-shrine at Elaeus in the Chersonese (9.116-20). His ships are later the first that Hector reaches and sets on fire (15.704-6, 16.286), a link that makes this brief entry part of the poem's design.

title: Philoctetes, abandoned on Lemnos
greek: Φιλοκτήτης … τόξων ἐῢ εἰδώς (Philoktētēs … toxōn eü eidōs); ἕλκεϊ … ὀλοόφρονος ὕδρου (helkei … oloophronos hudrou)
short: The great archer lies on 'sacred Lemnos' with a festering snake-bite, left behind by the Achaeans; 'soon' they will need him, a story outside the Iliad.
body: Philoctetes owned the bow of Heracles (a detail not in Homer) and was bitten by a water-snake (hudros) on the way to Troy; the smell of the wound and his cries led the Achaeans to maroon him on Lemnos. In the cyclic Cypria, as summarised by Proclus, the bite happens at Tenedos during a feast; in the Little Iliad an oracle reveals that Troy cannot fall without his bow, and Diomedes fetches him, after which he kills Paris. The Iliad's line 'yet full soon were the Argives beside their ships to bethink them of king Philoctetes' (2.724-5) points to that sequel. Sophocles' Philoctetes (409 BC) turns the episode into a drama about deceit and loyalty, with Odysseus and Achilles' son Neoptolemus; the play is the main reason the name is still familiar. Like Protesilaus and Achilles, he is a leader whose absence the Catalogue records.

title: Typhoeus and the land of the Arimi
greek: ὅτε τ᾽ ἀμφὶ Τυφωέϊ γαῖαν ἱμάσσῃ εἰν Ἀρίμοις, ὅθι φασὶ Τυφωέος ἔμμεναι εὐνάς (hote t' amphi Tuphōeï gaian himassēi ein Arimois, hothi phasi Tuphōeos emmenai eunas)
short: The earth groans under the marching army as when Zeus lashes the ground over the monster Typhoeus, buried 'among the Arimi'.
body: Typhoeus (Typhon) is the hundred-headed monster whom Zeus defeated with thunderbolts at the end of the struggle for power in Hesiod (Theogony 820-68); he was imagined as buried under the earth, where his movements cause earthquakes and volcanic fire. Homer's simile assumes the story is known. Where the Arimi were was disputed in antiquity: Strabo (13.4.6) lists claims for Cilicia, Syria, Lydia (Hyde or Sardis), the volcanic 'Burnt Land' (Katakekaumene) of Mysia and the Pithecussae islands off Italy, and Pindar places Typhon under both Cilicia and Etna (Pythian 1.15-28). Leaf, noting that one ancient text read Einarimois as a single word, concludes that Virgil must have read it so when he invented the island 'Inarime' (Aeneid 9.715-16), and that the Arimi are 'best located in mythland'. The simile is also cosmic: the army's tread is likened to the punishment of the enemy of Zeus's order.

title: Batieia, the 'barrow of Myrine'
greek: τὴν ἤτοι ἄνδρες Βατίειαν κικλήσκουσιν, ἀθάνατοι δέ τε σῆμα πολυσκάρθμοιο Μυρίνης (tēn ētoi andres Batieian kiklēskousin, athanatoi de te sēma poluskarthmoio Murinēs)
short: A mound on the Trojan plain with two names: men call it Batieia, the gods 'the barrow of Myrine, light of step', where the Trojans and allies muster.
body: This is another example of Homer's 'language of the gods' (compare Briareus-Aegaeon, 1.403-4). The human name, Batieia, may mean 'Brier Hill' (Leaf; from batos, 'bramble') or recall Batieia, daughter of Teucer and wife of Dardanus in later genealogy; the divine name makes it the tomb of Myrine, 'much-bounding' (poluskarthmos), whom later writers identified as an Amazon queen (Strabo 12.8.6; Diodorus 3.54-5). Such barrows were landmarks on the plain (compare the barrow of Aesyetes, 2.793, and of Ilus, 10.415), and the Trojan landscape of the poem is to a large degree a landscape of tombs. Leaf discusses whether the 'divine' names preserve older or foreign words.

title: 'Hector of the flashing helm' (koruthaiolos)
greek: μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ (megas koruthaiolos Hektōr)
short: Hector's commonest epithet: koruthaiolos, 'with glancing (or nodding) helmet', from korus, 'helmet', and aiolos, 'quick-moving, shimmering'.
body: Aiolos combines the ideas of rapid movement and changing light, so the epithet can mean 'with flashing helmet' or 'with waving plume'. It fits Hector as the moving centre of the Trojan army, and the helmet becomes a symbol in the most famous scene of Book 6, when his baby son Astyanax shrinks from the nodding horsehair crest and Hector takes the helmet off to hold him (6.466-73). Under him march 'the greatest hosts by far and the goodliest'. The Trojan Catalogue that begins here is much shorter and vaguer than the Achaean one (16 contingents, no ship numbers); Leaf observed its 'want of detailed knowledge', its arrangement along four lines radiating from Troy, and several differences from the rest of the Iliad. Hector's first action in the poem is to recognise Iris's voice and break up the assembly at once (2.807-8): a decisive leader, in contrast with Agamemnon's confused morning.

title: Aeneas, son of Aphrodite and Anchises
greek: Αἰνείας, τὸν ὑπ᾽ Ἀγχίσῃ τέκε δῖ᾽ Ἀφροδίτη Ἴδης ἐν κνημοῖσι θεὰ βροτῷ εὐνηθεῖσα (Aineias, ton hup' Ankhisēi teke di' Aphroditē Idēs en knēmoisi thea brotōi eunētheisa)
short: Leader of the Dardanians, born on Mount Ida to the goddess Aphrodite and the mortal Anchises; the Iliad already predicts that his line will survive Troy.
body: The Dardanians are a branch of the Trojan royal house, descended from Dardanus (whose name, Leaf notes, survives in 'Dardanelles'; the genealogy is given at 20.215-40); Aeneas' father Anchises is a cousin of Priam. The love of Aphrodite and Anchises, 'a goddess couched with a mortal man', is told at length in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (5.53-199), where Aphrodite prophesies that Aeneas and his descendants will rule the Trojans. The Iliad agrees: in Book 20, Poseidon rescues Aeneas from Achilles because he is fated to survive, and 'the might of Aeneas shall be king among the Trojans, and his sons' sons' (20.307-8). There is some tension with Priam's house in the poem (13.459-61). Roman writers built on these prophecies to make Aeneas the founder of the Roman race, above all in Virgil's Aeneid, so this short Catalogue entry introduces the hero of the most important epic written in Homer's wake.

title: The Carians 'of barbarous speech' (barbarophōnoi)
greek: Νάστης αὖ Καρῶν ἡγήσατο βαρβαροφώνων (Nastēs au Karōn hēgēsato barbarophōnōn)
short: The earliest appearance in Greek of the root barbar-: the Carians of Miletus speak a foreign tongue. The Trojan allies are many peoples of many languages.
body: Barbarophōnos means 'speaking unintelligibly, of foreign speech', from the imitative barbar ('bar-bar'). Leaf thought it referred only to the harshness of their dialect, like the Sintians 'of savage speech' (Od. 8.294). Thucydides (1.3.3) remarked that Homer nowhere uses the word 'barbarians', because the Greeks had not yet been marked off by a single name in contrast to others; Strabo (14.2.28) discussed this line at length, arguing that the word first referred to harsh or faulty speech. The Carians lived in south-west Asia Minor around Miletus, the Maeander and Mycale, later Ionian Greek territory. The Trojan Catalogue as a whole stresses linguistic variety: Iris tells Hector that 'tongue differs from tongue' among the scattered allies (2.804), and in Book 4 the Trojan army's clamour is likened to bleating sheep because their speech was mixed (4.433-8). The Achaeans, in contrast, speak as one people. Leaf, however, thought it absurd to imagine real language problems, since Greeks and Trojans converse freely throughout the poem, and suspected lines 2.803-4. He also remarks how effectively the poet evokes a remote past by casually calling the people of Miletus, later a great Greek city, barbarians. The Carian leader Nastes, who went to war 'decked with gold, like a girl', is judged 'fool' by the narrator.

title: Sarpedon and Glaucus, leaders of the Lycians
greek: Σαρπηδὼν δ᾽ ἦρχεν Λυκίων καὶ Γλαῦκος ἀμύμων τηλόθεν ἐκ Λυκίης, Ξάνθου ἄπο δινήεντος (Sarpēdōn d' ērkhen Lukiōn kai Glaukos amumōn tēlothen ek Lukiēs, Xanthou apo dinēentos)
short: The last entry of the Trojan Catalogue names the Lycians from the far south-west of Asia Minor, led by Sarpedon, son of Zeus, and Glaucus.
body: Lycia, on the river Xanthus (modern Eşen Çayı, near the site of Xanthos), is the most distant of the allied lands; Leaf notes that each line of the Trojan Catalogue ends with a people marked 'from afar' (tēle, tēlothen), and Lycia closes the southern line. Sarpedon is the greatest of the allies and a son of Zeus, and his two great moments define the heroic code: his speech to Glaucus on why kings must fight in the front rank to deserve their privileges and, since all men must die, should seek glory (12.310-28); and his death at the hands of Patroclus, when Zeus considers saving him from fate, is dissuaded by Hera, and weeps tears of blood (16.431-61). Glaucus meets Diomedes in Book 6, where the two discover an inherited guest-friendship (xenia) and exchange armour, gold for bronze (6.119-236). Ending the book with these two noble allies prepares for the human sympathy the poem extends to the Trojan side.
